first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are activation (-6%) and onboarding completion (-4%), so the onboarding-simplification family of memories (memory_86, reinforced by memory_31 and memory_91) is the most decision-consequential inherited belief. It is also insufficiently supported for the stated objective: memory_86 was measured on completion rate and time-to-value, which are proxies, not sustainable qualified revenue — shortening onboarding can raise completion while admitting weaker-fit accounts and stripping the qualification signal that memory_44 says matters for pipeline quality. So memory_86 is verified first: I want the original record's cohort, duration, and whether any revenue/retention endpoint was tracked. Second verification goes to memory_73 (promotional pricing), because the competitor's entry pricing creates strong pull toward a price response, and that memory is the one most likely to be misleading here: 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' says nothing about margin, discount-cohort retention, or whether the lift outlasted the promo window. Matching a price attack on the strength of an unverified short-horizon acquisition result is the highest-downside available move against a long-term revenue objective. I did not spend budget on memory_57 (referral incentives depend on an established, satisfied base — poor fit while activation is falling) or memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist is plausibly sound but addresses none of this week's declines). Current intent is simplify_onboarding at standard experiment scale, treated as provisional: it attacks both observed declines at once and is the least likely to buy revenue by degrading account quality. I am holding uncertainty open — if memory_86 turns out to rest on a narrow cohort or a pure completion-rate endpoint, activation_messaging (memory_91) becomes the safer substitute since it lifts engagement without altering the qualification funnel. Guardrails regardless of outcome: instrument downstream qualified-revenue and 30/90-day retention per cohort, not just completion, so this experiment does not consolidate another proxy-metric belief into memory.

final.rationale: Both verifications paid off, and in opposite directions. exp_86 came back stronger than the inherited summary: it tracked not only completion (+13%) and time-to-value (-2.1 days) but also a downstream endpoint — 30-day retention +3%. That is the specific concern I raised (that shortening onboarding might raise completion while admitting weaker-fit accounts) and it was directly measured and did not materialize. The retention lift means the added accounts were not worse-fit, so memory_86 is now supported for the sustainable-qualified-revenue objective, not just for proxies. exp_73 came back materially worse than the inherited summary and vindicates spending the second pull there: the archived record carries a retention of -12% and an explicit conclusion not to generalize targeted discounting as sustainable growth. The compressed memory had silently dropped that caveat and kept only 'strong acquisition and revenue lift.' Under a long-term objective, promotional_pricing is now ruled out despite being the most intuitive answer to a competitor price attack — it would buy signups that do not survive the first renewal cycle, which is the opposite of what is being optimized. So: simplify_onboarding, standard experiment scale. It is the only candidate that is both verified against a downstream endpoint and aimed at both observed declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%). I hold to standard scale rather than broad rollout: exp_86 ran in a different competitive environment than day 76, and its retention window was 30 days, which is short of a full renewal cycle — the same horizon limitation that made exp_73 look good before it looked bad. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving this week: whether onboarding simplification retains price-sensitive SMB accounts specifically, i.e. the segment actually being poached. It plausibly helps by improving time-to-value, but that is inference, not evidence. Guardrails: instrument per-cohort qualified revenue and retention past the first renewal boundary, not just 30 days, and segment results by price sensitivity so the competitor-exposed accounts are readable separately. Two memory-hygiene corrections to write back: amend memory_73 to carry the -12% retention and the do-not-generalize conclusion, since the lossy version is actively dangerous to any future agent facing a price attack; and note on memory_86 that its support includes a retention endpoint. If activation stays depressed after this, activation_messaging (memory_91) is the next probe — but memory_91 remains unverified and is a week-one engagement claim, so it should not be treated as revenue-grade evidence yet.
